passage_text: Researchers conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial to evaluate the efficacy of a novel antihypertensive agent, Hypotensol, in adults with stage 1 hypertension. Eighty participants were enrolled and randomly assigned to either the Hypotensol group (n=40) or a placebo group (n=40). Baseline systolic and diastolic blood pressures (BP) were measured after a 5‑minute seated rest. Participants received daily oral Hypotensol (20 mg) or identical placebo tablets for 4 weeks. BP readings were taken at the end of the study period. Table 1 summarizes the mean BP values and changes for both groups. The Hypotensol group exhibited a mean systolic BP reduction of 20 mmHg and a diastolic reduction of 10 mmHg, whereas the placebo group showed modest reductions of 3 mmHg systolic and 2 mmHg diastolic. The data suggest that Hypotensol effectively lowers BP compared to placebo, supporting its potential use as an adjunct therapy in hypertension management.
table_data:
Group | Baseline Systolic (mmHg) | Baseline Diastolic (mmHg) | 4‑week Systolic (mmHg) | 4‑week Diastolic (mmHg) | Change Systolic (mmHg) | Change Diastolic (mmHg)
Treatment | 150 | 95 | 130 | 85 | -20 | -10
Placebo | 148 | 92 | 145 | 90 | -3 | -2
stem: Which group experienced the greater absolute reduction in systolic blood pressure after 4 weeks of treatment?
explanation: The treatment group’s systolic BP decreased by 20 mmHg (from 150 to 130), whereas the placebo group’s systolic BP decreased by only 3 mmHg (from 148 to 145).
trap: The placebo group had a larger reduction in systolic BP.

stem: Which statement best describes the study design used in this research?
explanation: The investigators randomly assigned participants to treatment or placebo, blinded both participants and investigators, and used a placebo control, which defines a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
trap: Students may pick the observational cohort design because patients are followed over time, but random assignment, blinding and a placebo arm define an RCT.

stem: What is the percent reduction in mean systolic BP for the Hypotensol group?
explanation: Percent reduction = (20 mmHg ÷ 150 mmHg) × 100 % ≈ 13.3 %. The other options represent incorrect calculations or misinterpretations.
trap: 20% (interpreting the absolute change as a percent).

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data presented?

options.A: Hypotensol reduced systolic BP by 20 mmHg.
options.B: Placebo had no effect on diastolic BP.
options.C: Both groups had a reduction in diastolic BP.

explanation: The placebo group’s diastolic BP decreased by 2 mmHg (from 92 to 90 mmHg), indicating an effect. All other statements are supported by the data.
trap: Students accept 'placebo had no effect' because placebo changes look small, but diastolic BP fell 2 mmHg (92 to 90), so the statement overstates the null.

stem: Which conclusion is most directly supported by the study findings?

options.A: Hypotensol should replace all first‑line antihypertensives.
options.B: Over 4 weeks, Hypotensol lowered mean systolic and diastolic BP more than placebo in adults with stage 1 hypertension.
options.C: Hypotensol is ineffective in lowering BP.
options.D: Placebo is as effective as Hypotensol.

explanation: Correct: Systolic fell 20 vs 3 mmHg and diastolic 10 vs 2 mmHg with Hypotensol vs placebo. Why the others are wrong: A) No comparison with first-line drugs was made. C) BP fell clearly more than with placebo. D) The placebo changes (-3 and -2 mmHg) were far smaller.
trap: Students extend a short placebo-controlled trial to replacing first-line therapy or to use in other patients, but only the placebo comparison in stage 1 hypertension was tested.
